elevators.question: A step-free rider can use one of two elevators (or escalators) at the same station. Which one is more likely to be running this month?
method: Source: MTA NYCT Subway Elevator and Escalator Availability: Beginning 2015 (Metropolitan Transportation Authority, via data.ny.gov), retrieved 2026-10-19; 698 units, 140 months from Jan 2015.
Replay in time order. Each month's records reach memory only at the start of the next month; every decision reads only records valid before it (a check that throws on any later record found none).

Decisions: every month from Jan 2026 to Aug 2026, every pair of units of one kind at one station complex whose availability that month differs by more than half a point. Right means memory picked the unit that ran more.

No memory: a seeded coin. Placebo: every record ever read, kept forever (no validity window, no SUPERSEDES). Time-aware (Detour): records valid for 12 months, and a unit back from two months mostly out of service supersedes its older records, the way a superseded Finding is closed.
95% intervals: 2000 seeded bootstrap resamples of whole station complexes.

failureProne.question: Which 50 units will have the most unscheduled outages a month, Jan 2026 to Aug 2026?

failures.note: Memory predicts from the past; a unit that breaks for the first time, or one just repaired, still fools it. These are its largest misses.

stepFree.question: A wheelchair user asks for a step-free route. An elevator on the way is out of service, and memory knows it.
method: 40 accessible station-and-line platforms, taken at even steps from the 264 in the network (sorted by station and line); 0 already had an outage in memory and were skipped.

For each: report_elevator writes the outage as a Finding, then two step-free trips to and from an accessible station 3 to 8 stops along the line are routed with route_rider, once with memory off (outages ignored) and once on. The outage is then closed by a report that the elevator works again.
A trip counts when, with memory off, its route boards or leaves the train at the broken platform.

examples.trip: W 4 St-Wash Sq → Times Sq-42 St/Port Authority Bus Terminal

buses.question: A bus bridge is planned for so many riders an hour. How close does what it carries come to that?
method: 32 past shuttle incidents: 2 seeded (the L and A/C bridges) and 30 synthetic, six on each of 5 corridors whose buses carry a known share of plan (L 79%, A/C 93%, G 72%, 7 86%, J/Z 100%) give or take 6 points, from a seeded generator.

Leave one out: each incident is hidden, recall reads the rest from FalkorDB, and the bridge is sized the way the scripted controller sizes it: buses an hour divided by the lowest share of plan a recalled shuttle carried, when under 97%.
Without memory the buses run at the raw estimate. Carried = buses × 70 riders × the share that incident's buses really achieved; the error is its distance from the riders planned.
Online: the same rule fed only incidents that came earlier. 95% interval: seeded bootstrap over incidents.

sessions.question: Does a fact written in one session change what a later session answers?
method: Session A writes 6 facts through report_elevator: the L platform elevator at Myrtle-Wyckoff Avs works again (Aisha's), and outages at the busiest accessible stations (Grand Central-42 St 4, Times Sq-42 St/Port Authority Bus Terminal 1, Fulton St 2, 34 St-Herald Sq B, 34 St-Penn Station A).

Session B, a later request with a fresh context and another agent, asks 38 questions: every remembered rider's commute and 30 seeded step-free trips between accessible stations. Each answer is compared with the same question asked before session A.
Control: the same questions with memory off change nothing.

aisha.before: Aisha: about 33 min, 0 transfers, step-free: M Myrtle-Wyckoff Avs → 14 St/6 Av (11 stops). Skipped a faster path because memory says: Elevator to the L platform at Myrtle-Wyckoff Avs out of service; M platform elevator works.
aisha.after: Aisha: about 24 min, 0 transfers, step-free: L Myrtle-Wyckoff Avs → 14 St/6 Av (12 stops).

race.question: Many reports about one elevator arrive at once. Does memory end with exactly one current fact?
method: For 10, 50 and 100 writers: all report the same outage at once, then half report it fixed and half report it broken, all at once. Each writer is its own context; the open elevator facts for the platform are counted after each burst.
remember() writes the new finding and closes the one it supersedes in one query, and FalkorDB runs one write at a time per graph.
